data.title: Middle East Eye: Rohingya genocide case: How The Gambia went to The Hague and won
data.author: Sondos Asem
data.summary:
Rohingya genocide case: How The Gambia went to The Hague and won
Submitted by
Sondos Asem
on
Sun, 11/22/2026 - 15:04
Lead counsel Arsalan Suleman tells Middle East Eye how the small African country took Myanmar to court and how survivor testimony helped secure a landmark judgement
Eighty years after the International Court of Justice (ICJ) first sat in The Hague, I walked into the Peace Palace’s Great Hall of Justice to photograph the judges as they took their seats.
They were about to deliver a landmark judgment in a trailblazing case brought by The Gambia against Myanmar. For the first time, the court would find that a state had committed genocide, the "crime of all crimes" as it has been described.
It had been seven years since The Gambia, a slither of a country of less than three million people in West Africa that is named after the river that dissects it, filed the case.
It argued that Myanmar was trying to destroy the Rohingya, a predominantly Muslim minority that has lived in Rakhine State on the country's western coast for generations.
The case was brought under the 1948 Genocide Convention, the UN’s first human rights treaty, drawn up in the wake of the Holocaust to define genocide under international law and require states to prevent and punish it.
In the past, international criminal tribunals have convicted individuals of genocide, such as in courts created to prosecute atrocities committed during the wars in the former Yugoslavia and in Rwanda in the 1990s.
But this time the question before the ICJ, the UN’s highest court which adjudicates mainly in disputes between states, was whether Myanmar itself, as a state actor, can be held responsible.
In 2017, Myanmar’s military burned Rohingya villages, carried out mass killings and widespread rape, and deliberately killed children, the court found. Soldiers shot civilians as they fled, including people trying to swim to safety.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Yemen ministry puts losses from Saudi attacks and blockade above $1.13 trillion
data.author: Elis Gjevori
data.summary:
Yemen ministry puts losses from Saudi attacks and blockade above $1.13 trillion
Yemen’s Houthi-run Economy Ministry says Saudi attacks and the blockade have inflicted more than $1.13 trillion in cumulative economic losses since the war began began in March 2015.
Acting Economy Minister Sam al-Bashiri said preliminary estimates put direct damage during the latest escalation, from 13 July to 23 November, at more than $881.5m, Saba reports.
He said Saudi strikes destroyed 22 factories and partially damaged three others, causing industrial losses exceeding $376m.
The ministry put commercial losses above $85m and investment-sector losses above $20m.
Transport and Public Works Minister Mohammed Quhaim reported more than $350m in damage to infrastructure and other sectors during the same period.
Quhaim said attacks on airports, ports, roads and bridges had disrupted supplies and increased shipping, insurance and storage costs, placing further financial pressure on Yemenis.
The announcement provided no detailed methodology for the cumulative trillion-dollar estimate.

On Sunday, fraught global climate talks in Turkey, the longest ever in the climate conference’s history, ground to a halt, with no deal. The EU, UK and allies rejected the draft text over its failure to mention fossil fuels.

After delivering his intervention, O’Brien and EU Climate Minister Wopke Hoekstra walked out of the plenary to hold a press huddle while developing nations were speaking about the need for climate finance.

Houthis won't seize Aden, Yemeni government forces say
Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis have pushed as close as 60km to Aden, the temporary capital of the country's internationally recognised government, but they will not capture the city, Yemen's military said on Tuesday.
"I'll speak to you frankly. The situation is not where we want it to be. But it's not as dire as reported," Colonel Majed Abdullah Al-Nuzaily, spokesperson for Yemen's armed forces, told a group of reporters via video link.
Since fighting resumed in Yemen in July in parallel with the wider Iran war, the Houthis have rapidly advanced in Yemen, seizing territory from the internationally recognised government and its allies, who are backed by Saudi Arabia.
The Saudis have carried out air strikes on Yemen in support of their allies on the ground, while the Houthis have struck Saudi oil targets, airports and office towers.
Aden, now the target of Houthi missile and drone strikes, had previously not seen major hostilities since street battles in 2015, soon after the internationally recognised government fled Houthi-run Sanaa and made the port city its base.

data.title: Middle East Eye: US judge permanently bars Trump from punishing rights groups who liaise with ICC
data.author: MEE staff
data.summary:
US judge permanently bars Trump from punishing rights groups who liaise with ICC
Submitted by
MEE staff
on
Tue, 11/24/2026 - 16:42
The president's executive order had put several US-based organisations at risk of fines and prison time
The International Criminal Court in The Hague (Remko De Waal/ANP/AFP)
Off
A US federal judge on Monday permanently barred the Trump administration from punishing rights groups who liaise with the International Criminal Court (ICC).
The ruling extends to all Americans, and not just the plaintiffs in the case.
Judge Jesse Furman of the Southern District of New York first issued a temporary injunction last month.
This week he ruled that while "the Government effectively requests that the Court reconsider its earlier decisions ... there is no merit to that request".
"Put simply, Plaintiffs demonstrate that the Services Prohibition is a content-based restriction on speech and that it is not narrowly tailored to serve compelling state interests," Furman wrote.
Democracy for the Arab World Now (Dawn), founded by the late Middle East Eye columnist Jamal Khashoggi, filed the lawsuit in July.
In October, Furman blocked the Trump administration from potentially imposing civil or criminal liability on the group as well as another allied organisation, the Taxpayer Alliance Against Genocide (Taag), for any work carried out with the ICC.
"Anyone violating this prohibition could face up to 20 years in prison and up to $1 million in civil fines," Dawn said in a press release on Tuesday.
"Because the government can interpret the term 'services' to encompass anything that confers a benefit on the recipient, Americans before this ruling risked criminal prosecution for submitting evidence about possible crimes to the ICC, or for exchanging information with and engaging in joint advocacy with the Palestinian human rights groups and Special Rapporteur [Francesca] Albanese."

data.title: Middle East Eye: IRGC says it attacked container ship in Strait of Hormuz
data.author: Bilge Kotan
data.summary:
IRGC says it attacked container ship in Strait of Hormuz
The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said its navy targeted a container ship in the Strait of Hormuz.
The IRGC said in a statement that it switched off its navigation and positioning systems, and the ship was “illegally” transiting through a restricted area north of Khasab in Oman.
“[We] once again emphasise to the owners and commanders of commercial vessels that adhering to maritime safety regulations, using authorised routes, and paying attention to warnings issued by relevant authorities are essential for ensuring the safety of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz,” the statement said.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Germany's left-wing Die Linke party expels pro-Palestine lawmaker
data.author: Bilge Kotan
data.summary:
Germany's left-wing Die Linke party expels pro-Palestine lawmaker
Germany's far-left Die Linke party on Tuesday expelled local pro-Palestine lawmaker Vanessa Emde over her criticism of Israel.
Die Linke, which came first in local elections in Berlin in September, has been trying to hammer out a coalition deal with the centre-left Social Democrats (SPD) and the Greens.
Emde was newly elected as a local representative from the Neukolln district, which has a large Arab population.
Emde's expulsion on Tuesday - which was backed by more than two-thirds of Die Linke's lawmakers in the Berlin parliament - clears one potential hurdle to sealing a coalition deal with the SPD and the Greens.
